title: Work done by a field
objectives: Compute the work a field does along a path.

screens.title: Where does the field help
screens.prose: The field $\mathbf F = (0, x)$ has vertical arrows that grow to the right. Three paths run from $(0, 0)$ to $(1, 1)$. A goes along the $x$-axis then up, B up then along, D straight.
screens.question: Tap the straight piece where the arrows push hardest along the direction of travel.

hints.text: Compare the arrows' direction with each piece's direction.
On the line $x = 1$ the arrows are longest and point up.
The upward piece of path A runs along $x = 1$.

feedback.correct: On the upward piece of A the arrows point exactly along the motion, at full strength.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find a piece where the arrows point the same way as the motion.

byKey.diag: On the diagonal the arrows meet the path at 45 degrees, so only part of each push counts.
byKey.b-up: On the $y$-axis $x = 0$, so the field is zero there.
byKey.flat: Along the $x$-axis the arrows point up, at right angles to the motion: no push along it.
byKey.top: Along the top the arrows point up, at right angles to the motion: no push along it.

explain.text: On $x = 1$ the arrow is $(0, 1)$, pointing up the path, so every step gets the full push. On horizontal pieces the vertical arrows push across the path, never along it.

screens.title: Add up the pushes
screens.prose: On a straight piece, only the part of the arrow along the motion does work. On a horizontal piece that part is $P$, on a vertical piece $Q$. Add up push times distance along each path.
screens.question: Fill in the work done by $\mathbf F = (0, x)$ along each path.

hints.text: On horizontal pieces $P = 0$, so they add nothing.
On A's upward piece $Q = x = 1$ over a distance 1. On B's, $Q = x = 0$.
On D, $\mathbf r = (t, t)$: the push per unit $t$ is $Q \cdot 1 = t$, and $\int_0^1 t\,dt = \tfrac12$.

feedback.correct: A gives 1, B gives 0 and D gives $\tfrac12$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the upward pieces: what is $x$ on each?

byKey.swap-a: On A's upward piece $x = 1$, so the push is 1 over a distance 1.
byKey.swap-b: On B's upward piece $x = 0$, so the field is zero there.
byKey.scalar: You used the arrow's full length $|\mathbf F| = t$ times the speed $\sqrt 2$. Only the part along the motion counts: $(0, t) \cdot (1, 1) = t$.

explain.text: A gives $0 + \int_0^1 1\,dy = 1$, B gives $0 + 0 = 0$ and D gives $\int_0^1 t\,dt = \tfrac12$. Same ends, three different totals.

screens.title: Only the tangential part counts
screens.prose: Adding push times distance along a curve gives the **work** $$W = \int_C \mathbf F \cdot d\mathbf r = \int_a^b \mathbf F(\mathbf r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t)\,dt,$$ also written $\int_C P\,dx + Q\,dy$. The picture projects $\mathbf F$ onto $\mathbf r'$: only that part counts.
screens.question: Take $\mathbf F = (y, x)$ along $\mathbf r(t) = (t, t^2)$. Write the integrand $\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t)$ in terms of $t$.

hints.text: $\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t)) = (t^2, t)$.
$\mathbf r'(t) = (1, 2t)$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Dot $\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t)) = (t^2, t)$ with $\mathbf r'(t) = (1, 2t)$.

byKey.no-rprime: You dotted with $(1, 1)$, the velocity at $t = 0.5$ only. In general $\mathbf r'(t) = (1, 2t)$.

explain.text: $\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t)) = (t^2, t)$ and $\mathbf r'(t) = (1, 2t)$, so the dot product is $3t^2$. It is the tangential part of $\mathbf F$ times the speed.

screens.title: Work along a parabola
screens.prose: Now integrate: $W = \int_0^1 3t^2\,dt$ along the parabola. The dashed line $y = x$ joins the same ends.
screens.question: What is the work of $\mathbf F = (y, x)$ along $y = x^2$ from $(0, 0)$ to $(1, 1)$?

hints.text: Integrate $3t^2$ from 0 to 1.
$\left[t^3\right]_0^1$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Integrate the integrand $3t^2$ over $0 \le t \le 1$.

byKey.no-rprime: You integrated $t^2 + t$, using $\mathbf r' = (1, 1)$. Along the parabola $\mathbf r' = (1, 2t)$.

explain.text: $W = 1$. Along $y = x$, $\mathbf r = (t, t)$ gives $\int_0^1 2t\,dt = 1$ too. Lesson 4 explains when every path gives the same work.

screens.title: Round a circle
screens.prose: The rotation field $(-y, x)$ again, round the unit circle $\mathbf r(t) = (\cos t, \sin t)$, $0 \le t \le 2\pi$, counterclockwise. The small arrows show the direction of travel.
screens.question: What is the work $\oint_C \mathbf F \cdot d\mathbf r$?

hints.text: $\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t)) = (-\sin t, \cos t)$.
$\mathbf r'(t) = (-\sin t, \cos t)$ too.
The dot product is $\sin^2 t + \cos^2 t = 1$; integrate over $2\pi$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Dot $\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))$ with $\mathbf r'(t)$ first.

byKey.zero: You expected a closed path to give 0. Here the arrows push along the path all the way round.
byKey.half: $\pi$ is half a turn. The integral runs over the full $0 \le t \le 2\pi$.

explain.text: $\mathbf F$ and $\mathbf r'$ are equal here, so the integrand is $|\mathbf r'|^2 = 1$. The work is $2\pi$, though the path ends where it began.

screens.title: A closed path with no work
screens.prose: Now the outward field $(x, y)$ round the same circle, counterclockwise. The arrows are far from zero, yet the work is 0.
screens.question: Why is the work 0?

options.text: $\mathbf F$ is at right angles to the path at every point
The path is closed, so the work is always 0
options.why: The rotation field gave $2\pi$ on this same closed path.

options.text: $\mathbf F$ is zero on the circle
options.why: At $(1, 0)$ the field is $(1, 0)$, not zero.

options.text: Positive and negative parts cancel round the loop
options.why: Nothing cancels: every piece is exactly 0, as $(\cos t, \sin t) \cdot (-\sin t, \cos t) = 0$.

hints.text: Compare $\mathbf F$ with the direction of travel.
$\mathbf F = (\cos t, \sin t)$ and $\mathbf r' = (-\sin t, \cos t)$.
Their dot product is 0 at every $t$.

feedback.correct: Every arrow points across the path, so no piece does any work.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out $\mathbf F \cdot \mathbf r'$ at one point.

explain.text: $(\cos t, \sin t) \cdot (-\sin t, \cos t) = 0$ for every $t$. A field at right angles to the path does no work, however strong it is.

screens.title: The dx, dy form
screens.prose: $\int_C P\,dx + Q\,dy$ means $\int_a^b \big(P\,x'(t) + Q\,y'(t)\big)\,dt$. Take the segment from $(0, 0)$ to $(2, 1)$, $\mathbf r(t) = (2t, t)$.
screens.question: What is $\int_C y\,dx + x^2\,dy$, to 3 decimal places?

hints.text: $dx = x'(t)\,dt = 2\,dt$ and $dy = dt$.
$y\,dx = 2t\,dt$ and $x^2\,dy = 4t^2\,dt$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Replace $dx$ by $x'(t)\,dt$ and $dy$ by $y'(t)\,dt$.

explain.text: $dx = 2\,dt$ and $dy = dt$, so the integrand is $2t + 4t^2$. Integrating gives $1 + \tfrac43 = \tfrac73 \approx 2.333$.

screens.title: Work in space
screens.prose: In space, $W = \int_a^b \mathbf F(\mathbf r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t)\,dt$ with three entries. Take $\mathbf F = (y, z, x)$ along the helix $\mathbf r(t) = (\cos t, \sin t, t)$, $0 \le t \le 2\pi$. Rotate to see the field along it.
screens.question: What is $\int_C \mathbf F \cdot d\mathbf r$?

hints.text: $\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t)) = (\sin t, t, \cos t)$ and $\mathbf r'(t) = (-\sin t, \cos t, 1)$.
The dot product is $-\sin^2 t + t\cos t + \cos t$.
$\int_0^{2\pi} -\sin^2 t\,dt = -\pi$; the other two terms integrate to 0.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Dot the three entries and integrate each term.

byKey.pos: Check the first term: $y \cdot x'(t) = \sin t \cdot (-\sin t) = -\sin^2 t$, which gives $-\pi$.

explain.text: $\int_0^{2\pi} t\cos t\,dt = \left[t\sin t + \cos t\right]_0^{2\pi} = 0$ and $\int_0^{2\pi} \cos t\,dt = 0$. Only $-\sin^2 t$ survives, giving $-\pi$.

screens.title: Direction matters now
screens.prose: The rotation field $(-y, x)$ round the unit circle once more, but **clockwise**: $\mathbf r(t) = (\cos t, -\sin t)$, $0 \le t \le 2\pi$.
screens.question: What is the work clockwise?

options.text: $2\pi$, since direction never matters in a line integral
options.why: You carried over lesson 2, where $ds$ is a length. Here $d\mathbf r$ carries direction, so reversing the path flips the sign.

canvas.caption: This is the counterclockwise direction, the one that gives 2π.

options.text: $2\pi$, since $|\mathbf F| = 1$ and the circle has length $2\pi$
options.why: That is $\int_C |\mathbf F|\,ds$. Work uses the dot product, and clockwise each dot product is $-1$.
Counterclockwise gave $2\pi$ on the same closed path, so closed does not force 0.

hints.text: Does the motion now go with the arrows or against them?
$\mathbf r'(t) = (-\sin t, -\cos t)$ and $\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t)) = (\sin t, \cos t)$.
The dot product is $-1$; integrate over $2\pi$.

feedback.correct: Against the arrows all the way: $W = -2\pi$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out $\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t)$ for the clockwise path.

byKey.l2: You treated work like lesson 2's $\int f\,ds$, which ignores direction. Work along $-C$ is minus the work along $C$.
byKey.scalar: You integrated the arrow length $|\mathbf F| = 1$. Work counts only the part along the motion, here $-1$.

explain.text: Clockwise, $\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t)) = (\sin t, \cos t)$ and $\mathbf r'(t) = (-\sin t, -\cos t)$, so the integrand is $-1$. Reversing a path flips the sign of its work.

screens.title: Along a flow line
screens.prose: On a flow line the path moves with the arrows, so the dot product is $|\mathbf F|\,|\mathbf r'|$ and $W = \int_C |\mathbf F|\,ds$. Take the rotation field round the circle of radius 2, counterclockwise.
screens.question: What is the work round the circle of radius 2?

hints.text: On this circle $|\mathbf F| = |(-y, x)| = 2$.
The circle's length is $4\pi$.
$W = 2 \times 4\pi$.

feedback.correct: $|\mathbf F| = 2$ all the way round a path of length $4\pi$: $W = 8\pi$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the arrow length on the circle by the circle's length.

byKey.length: $4\pi$ is the length alone. On this circle each arrow has length 2, so double it.
byKey.unit: $2\pi$ is the unit circle's answer. Here the radius 2 doubles both the arrows and the length.

explain.text: With $\mathbf r = (2\cos t, 2\sin t)$ the integrand is $(-2\sin t)^2 + (2\cos t)^2 = 4$. So $W = 4 \times 2\pi = 8\pi$, the arrow length 2 times the length $4\pi$.

screens.title: Work numerically
screens.prose: Write `work(F, r, r_prime, a, b)`, returning $\int_a^b \mathbf F(\mathbf r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t)\,dt$ with `quad`. It must work in the plane and in space. The tests reuse this lesson's paths, including the hook's two corner paths.
screens.question: Complete `work`.

widget.starter:
import math
from scipy.integrate import quad


def work(F, r, r_prime, a, b):
    """Return the work of F along r(t), a <= t <= b.

    F(p) takes a point p as a tuple and returns a tuple
    of the same length. r(t) and r_prime(t) return tuples.
    quad(g, a, b) returns (value, error estimate).
    """
    pass

examples.call: work(lambda p: (-p[1], p[0]), lambda t: (math.cos(t), math.sin(t)), lambda t: (-math.sin(t), math.cos(t)), 0, 2*math.pi)

tests.call: work(lambda p: (-p[1], p[0]), lambda t: (math.cos(t), math.sin(t)), lambda t: (-math.sin(t), math.cos(t)), 0, 2*math.pi)
work(lambda p: (-p[1], p[0]), lambda t: (math.cos(t), -math.sin(t)), lambda t: (-math.sin(t), -math.cos(t)), 0, 2*math.pi)
work(lambda p: (p[0], p[1]), lambda t: (math.cos(t), math.sin(t)), lambda t: (-math.sin(t), math.cos(t)), 0, 2*math.pi)
work(lambda p: (p[1], p[0]), lambda t: (t, t*t), lambda t: (1, 2*t), 0, 1)
work(lambda p: (p[1], p[0]**2), lambda t: (2*t, t), lambda t: (2, 1), 0, 1)
work(lambda p: (p[1], p[2], p[0]), lambda t: (math.cos(t), math.sin(t), t), lambda t: (-math.sin(t), math.cos(t), 1), 0, 2*math.pi)
work(lambda p: (0, p[0]), lambda t: (t, 0), lambda t: (1, 0), 0, 1) + work(lambda p: (0, p[0]), lambda t: (1, t), lambda t: (0, 1), 0, 1)
work(lambda p: (0, p[0]), lambda t: (0, t), lambda t: (0, 1), 0, 1) + work(lambda p: (0, p[0]), lambda t: (t, 1), lambda t: (1, 0), 0, 1)

widget.how: Check runs 8 hidden tests, each accepted within absolute 1e-6. SciPy loads on the first run; it took about 7 s in testing.

hints.text: Build $g(t) = \mathbf F(\mathbf r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t)$.
`sum(f * d for f, d in zip(F(r(t)), r_prime(t)))` is the dot product in any dimension.
Return `quad(g, a, b)[0]`.

feedback.correct: All 8 tests pass: both directions round the circle, the helix and both corner paths.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test.

byKey.test-2: Test 2 is clockwise and expects $-2\pi$. A version using $|\mathbf F|\,|\mathbf r'|$ gets $2\pi$ here.
byKey.test-6: Test 6 is in space: zip the three entries, not just two.

explain.text: The dot product uses every entry, so one function handles the plane and space. Reversing $\mathbf r$ flips the sign of $\mathbf r'$ and so of the work.

screens.title: P&L along a price path
screens.prose: Two stocks start at £100 and end at £110 and £105. A rule holds $S_1 - 100$ shares of stock 2 and none of stock 1: holdings $\mathbf h = (0, S_1 - 100)$. Its P&L along a price path is $\int \mathbf h \cdot d\mathbf S$.
screens.question: Fill in the P&L for each order of moves.

hints.text: Only moves in stock 2 earn anything: $\mathbf h$ holds no stock 1.
How many shares of stock 2 are held while stock 2 moves?
Stock 1 first: $110 - 100 = 10$ shares gain £5 each. Stock 2 first: 0 shares.

feedback.correct: £50 if stock 1 moves first, £0 if stock 2 moves first.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the stock 2 shares held while stock 2 moves.

byKey.swap-1: When stock 2 moves last, $S_1$ is already 110, so 10 shares are held.
byKey.swap-2: When stock 2 moves first, $S_1 = 100$, so the rule holds 0 shares.

explain.text: Stock 1 first: 10 shares of stock 2 gain £5 each, £50. Stock 2 first: no shares are held while it moves, £0. Same start and end prices, different P&L: this is the hook's field.

ideas: Work is $\int_C \mathbf F \cdot d\mathbf r = \int_a^b \mathbf F(\mathbf r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t)\,dt$: only the part of $\mathbf F$ along the motion counts.
Reversing the path flips the sign of the work, unlike $\int_C f\,ds$.
A field at right angles to the path does no work. Paths with the same ends can give different work.

formula.name: Work
formula.tex: W = \int_C P\,dx + Q\,dy = \int_a^b \mathbf F(\mathbf r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t)\,dt

summary.trap: Carrying lesson 2's rule that direction does not matter into a work integral.

quiz.prose: $\mathbf F = (1, 0)$ everywhere. $C$ is the segment from $(0, 0)$ to $(3, 2)$, $\mathbf r(t) = (3t, 2t)$.
quiz.question: What is $\int_C \mathbf F \cdot d\mathbf r$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Dot $\mathbf F$ with $\mathbf r'(t) = (3, 2)$.

byKey.length: That is $\int |\mathbf F|\,ds$, the length $\sqrt{13}$. Only the part along $x$ counts.

explain.text: The integrand is $(1, 0) \cdot (3, 2) = 3$, so $W = 3$: the field only pushes along $x$, and $x$ rises by 3.

quiz.prose: The work of a field along a path $C$ from $A$ to $B$ is 5.
quiz.question: What is the work along the same curve from $B$ back to $A$?

feedback.correct: Reversing the path flips the sign: $-5$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about what reversing does to $\mathbf r'$.

byKey.same: You kept lesson 2's rule. In $\int \mathbf F \cdot d\mathbf r$ reversing flips $\mathbf r'$, so the work changes sign.

explain.text: Reversed, every $\mathbf r'$ points the other way, so each dot product changes sign. The work becomes $-5$.

quiz.prose: $C$ is the unit circle $(\cos t, \sin t)$, $0 \le t \le 2\pi$, counterclockwise.
quiz.question: What is $\oint_C x\,dy$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put $x = \cos t$ and $dy = \cos t\,dt$.

byKey.zero: $\cos^2 t$ is never negative, so nothing cancels. It averages $\tfrac12$ over $2\pi$.

explain.text: $x\,dy = \cos t \cdot \cos t\,dt$, and $\cos^2 t$ averages $\tfrac12$ over a full turn. So the integral is $\pi$.

quiz.question: Which integral is the work of $\mathbf F$ along $\mathbf r(t)$, $a \le t \le b$?

options.why: That counts the whole arrow. Work counts only the part along the motion.
The dot with $\mathbf r'$ already carries the speed; this counts it twice.
$\mathbf F$ takes a point. Evaluate it at $\mathbf r(t)$, not at $t$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work is the tangential part of $\mathbf F$ added along the path.

explain.text: $\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t)$ is the tangential part of $\mathbf F$ times the speed. Integrating in $t$ adds it along the path.
